Electric Skates vs Hoverboards: What's the Difference and Which Is Better?

# Electric Skates vs Hoverboards: What's the Difference and Which Is Better?

AIRTRICK

Oct 26

Last updated: October 2026

## Electric Skates vs Hoverboards: The Short Answer

Electric skates are worn on your feet and ride on wheels, while a hoverboard is a self-balancing platform you stand on without straps. Electric skates have four wheels per skate, an ankle strap, and a handheld remote that controls speed and braking. A hoverboard balances itself with gyroscopes and needs no controller. They look like cousins in photos. In use, they are not the same thing at all.

The practical difference comes down to control. On a hoverboard you steer by leaning. On electric skates you steer with your body but control speed and braking with a 2.4G remote in your hand. That single design choice changes who can ride them, where they fit, and how safe they feel on a real street.

## How Each One Actually Works

Electric skates — You keep your own sneakers on and step onto the frame. Two nylon Velcro straps and a rotating ankle support lock your foot down. Each skate has four PU wheels (58 mm front, 68 mm rear) with a hub motor driving them, plus an electronic brake and a yellow physical stopper at the heel. The battery sits in a box under the frame. Turn the rear wheel and the system powers on.

Hoverboards — Two motorized wheels on either side of a platform, with gyroscopes and accelerometers keeping the deck level. Lean forward to go, lean back to stop, twist your feet to turn. There is no strap, no controller, and no way to keep your feet from stepping off mid-ride.

## Electric Skates vs Hoverboards: Side by Side

Riding position — Electric skates: standing on two independent skates, feet strapped in, one foot slightly ahead of the other. Hoverboard: both feet side by side on a single deck, unstrapped.

Top speed — Electric skates: 15 mph (25 km/h) on the A1 Pro, 20 mph (32 km/h) on the A1 Ultra. Hoverboards: typically 6-10 mph, with most budget models capped near 6 mph.

Range — Electric skates: 9 miles (15 km) on the A1 Pro, 15.5 miles (25 km) on the A1 Ultra. Hoverboards: 6-12 miles on most adult models, less on cheaper units.

Weight — Electric skates: 3.5 lbs (1.65 kg) per skate on the A1 Pro, 3.9 lbs (1.9 kg) on the A1 Ultra, so about 7-8 lbs for the pair. Hoverboards: 22-26 lbs for a single unit.

Folded footprint — Electric skates: ankle supports rotate flat, the two frames press face to face, and the pair slides into the included dust bag. Hoverboards: no folding. There is a handle on some models and that is it.

Learning time — Electric skates: 30-60 minutes for a first-time rider, starting in the 6 mph low mode. Hoverboards: roughly 10 minutes to stop wobbling, though balance confidence takes longer.

Braking — Electric skates: electronic brake on the remote plus a physical heel stopper to lift your toe into. Hoverboards: lean back and let the gyros slow the wheels. No separate brake, no lever.

Price — Electric skates: $599 for the A1 Pro and $599 for the A1 Ultra (currently promoted down from $699). Hoverboards: $150-500 for most consumer models, with cheap units clustering near $180.

Battery certification — Electric skates: UL 2272, UL, CE, FCC, RoHS, and each pack stays under 100Wh so it clears TSA carry-on rules. Hoverboards: UL 2272 exists for this category too, but a large share of budget boards still ship from sellers who skip it, which is why the standard exists in the first place.

## The Core Difference Is Stability, Not Speed

Hoverboards feel stable right up until they don't. The deck stays level on its own, so beginners think they have it after two minutes — then a crack in the pavement shifts weight to one foot and the board pivots under them.

Electric skates go the other way. At first you feel every wobble, because both feet are strapped to separate platforms and your ankles do the balancing. Ten minutes in, your legs figure it out. The payoff is that each skate is an independent four-wheel platform with a long wheelbase, so a pothole hits two wheels instead of tipping a whole deck.

It is the difference between standing on a moving platform and wearing one. Skaters prefer the second once they get past the first half hour.

## Portability: The Category Split Nobody Talks About

You cannot put a hoverboard in a backpack. At 22-26 lbs with no folding mechanism, it goes in a trunk, on a shelf, or in your hand for the walk into class.

A pair of electric skates weighs 7-8 lbs and compresses as small as two lunchboxes stacked. The frame is 309 x 66.5 x 126 mm. Riders carry them in the dust bag, on the subway, into lectures, through airport security, and up apartment stairs without thinking about it.

That is also why electric skates solve the last-mile problem and hoverboards usually don't. If the ride can't come indoors with you, the trip has to be a loop that starts and ends at the same doorway.

## Learning Curve: 30-60 Minutes vs 10 Minutes

Credit where it's due — hoverboards are quicker to stand on. Ten minutes and most people can move in a straight line.

Electric skates take longer, and the honest number is 30-60 minutes spread across a couple of sessions. Start in low mode at 6 mph (10 km/h) on flat pavement, wear a helmet and pads, and practice the two things that matter: lean forward when you accelerate, lean back when you brake. Do that and the rest comes fast.

Our guide to braking on electric skates covers the weight-shift part in more detail if the stopping end worries you.

## Which Is Safer?

Neither is foolproof. Both put you on small wheels at speed near car traffic. But the failure modes are different.

Hoverboards fail in two ways: the battery, and the sudden dismount. Cheap lithium packs have caused fires and recalls, and a board that stops balancing gives you no time to react because your feet were never attached.

Electric skates fail like skates do — you lose an edge, catch a pebble, or lean the wrong way. The upside is that a rider strapped into an ankle support can usually recover or step into a fall, and the electronic brake plus heel stopper gives two stopping options instead of one lean.

One more point on riding surfaces: neither belongs on wet pavement. Small wheels and slick asphalt are a bad combination, so treat both as dry-weather machines.

## Which One Should You Buy?

Buy a hoverboard if — you want a toy for a driveway or a park loop, the rider is a kid, you'll never carry it more than fifty feet, and the budget is under $300.

Buy electric skates if — you actually have somewhere to go. Commuting, campus, train stations, apartment living, an e-scooter ban in your city, or a bag that already carries your laptop. The A1 Ultra covers 15.5 miles at up to 20 mph and weighs 3.9 lbs per skate. The A1 Pro is the lighter-duty version at 15 mph and 9 miles, and it climbs a 16% grade while the Ultra handles 22%.

If you are somewhere in between — curious, but not ready to commit — the cheaper A1 Pro is the sane entry point. Same frame, same straps, same 30-60 minute learning curve, less top end.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### Is an electric skate the same as a hoverboard?

No. They are different product categories that happen to share small wheels and a battery. A hoverboard is a single self-balancing platform with no straps and no controller. Electric roller skates are two separate wheeled frames you strap your shoes into, with a remote for throttle and braking.

### Which is easier to learn, electric skates or a hoverboard?

Hoverboards win that one — about 10 minutes to stand and move. Electric skates take 30-60 minutes because you balance on two independent platforms rather than one deck. The trade is that skate control is more precise once it clicks, since speed and braking come from a remote instead of weight guessing.

### Are electric skates better than hoverboards for commuting?

Yes, and portability is the reason. A pair of A1 skates weighs 7-8 lbs and folds into a bag small enough for a backpack, so they come into the office or the lecture hall with you. A 22-26 lb hoverboard stays outside, which rules out one-way trips.

### Which is safer, electric skates or a hoverboard?

Electric skates give you more ways out of trouble: an electronic brake, a physical heel stopper, and an ankle strap that keeps your feet connected to the platform. Hoverboards rely on a single lean-based braking system, and budget models have a long history of battery fires and recalls. Both are dry-pavement machines with helmet-and-pads rules.

### Can you take electric skates on a plane?

Yes, as carry-on. Each battery pack stays under the 100Wh limit that TSA allows in the cabin, so the skates travel with you rather than in checked baggage. Hoverboards generally get refused at the gate for exactly this reason — most packs blow past the limit.

## Start Rolling

Two very different machines. If you want a toy, buy the toy. If you want to actually get somewhere and still have fun doing it, the A1 series is built for that — 3.9 lbs, 20 mph, and a backpack-friendly footprint.
